title: Jio, NSE and Zepto Are All Going Public at Once. India's Market Has Never Absorbed ₹70,000 Crore in a Single Window.
excerpt: Three mega IPOs — a telecom giant, a stock exchange monopoly, and a quick-commerce upstart — are about to test whether India's primary market can swallow the biggest listing pipeline in its history.
body:
India is about to do something it has never done before: launch three initial public offerings in the same market window that together could raise more than ₹70,000 crore. Jio Platforms, the National Stock Exchange, and quick-commerce upstart Zepto have all filed their draft papers. If India's primary market was a runway, three of its heaviest aircraft just taxied onto it at once.

The centrepiece is Jio Platforms. Mukesh Ambani's telecom and digital juggernaut filed a draft red herring prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Board of India earlier this month for what would be India's largest-ever initial public offering. The company plans to issue up to 27 crore fresh equity shares — no existing shareholder is selling — and is expected to raise approximately ₹35,000 crore, eclipsing Hyundai Motor India's ₹27,859 crore record from 2024.

SEBI has since sought clarifications on the filing, asking for additional details on disclosures and fund allocation. The query is routine — every major IPO goes through it — but it means Jio's listing is unlikely before late 2026 at the earliest, since the regulator must issue its final observations before a price band can be set.

What makes Jio's offering unusual is its structure. Of the twenty largest IPOs in Indian history, fifteen were majority offer-for-sale, where existing shareholders cash out. Nine were entirely OFS. Jio is doing the opposite: every rupee raised goes into the company, primarily to retire ₹27,500 crore in debt held by subsidiary Reliance Jio Infocomm. None of Jio's marquee backers — Meta, Google, KKR, Mubadala, or the Saudi Public Investment Fund — are selling a single share. That's a vote of confidence, not an exit.

Running in parallel is the National Stock Exchange's long-delayed listing. NSE's IPO sits at the other extreme: it is a pure offer-for-sale, with existing shareholders — including the State Bank of India and the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board — divesting roughly six per cent of the exchange. The company itself receives nothing. Based on unlisted-market valuations, the offering could be worth around ₹30,000 crore, potentially making it India's second-largest public issue.

Then there is Zepto. The quick-commerce firm, founded by two Mumbai teenagers in 2021, has filed for an IPO combining a ₹8,010 crore fresh issue with an offer-for-sale by early backers including Nexus Venture. Co-founders Aadit Palicha and Kaivalya Vohra are not selling.

The three companies tell very different stories about what their investors want. Jio is paying down debt with new capital and signalling a multi-year growth bet. NSE is letting long-locked shareholders finally take profits from India's exchange monopoly. Zepto is simultaneously raising growth capital and giving venture backers a partial exit after years of losses. One IPO funds the balance sheet, one monetises it, and the third tries to do both.

The question is whether the market can digest all of it. Foreign portfolio investors have pulled a record $30.6 billion from Indian equities so far this year. Monsoon rains are running 43 per cent below average, dimming sentiment. But crude oil has crashed from $126 to below $73 as the Strait of Hormuz reopened, and Reliance shares rose after the company's annual general meeting signalled Jio and its AI ambitions as core growth pillars.

For the Indian diaspora, this pipeline represents a rare chance to participate directly in companies that define daily life across the subcontinent. Jio's 500 million-plus subscribers make it the dominant digital utility. NSE processes virtually every equity trade in the country. Zepto is rewriting how urban Indians buy groceries. NRIs investing through GIFT City's International Financial Services Centre can now access Indian IPOs through a regulated gateway — a route that has seen inflows roughly double over the past year, according to industry estimates.

Several more offerings are stacking up behind the big three. SBI Mutual Fund has filed for a ₹10,000 crore IPO. Insurtech firm Acko and dairy brand Milky Mist are in the pipeline. Kuku FM, PocketFM's rival in audio entertainment, has confidentially filed for a ₹2,500–3,500 crore issue. The second half of 2026 could see the highest concentration of large Indian listings in a single calendar year.

But it is Jio that will set the tone. At a rumoured valuation of $120–180 billion, it would not only be India's biggest IPO but a test of whether global investors are willing to price India's digital infrastructure at Silicon Valley multiples. If Jio prices well, every listing behind it gets a tailwind. If it stumbles, the queue may thin quickly.

*Sources: SEBI filings; Outlook Money; Hindu BusinessLine; Livemint; Reuters*

nri_angle: NRIs can invest in Indian IPOs through GIFT City, and Jio's listing gives the diaspora its first chance to directly own shares in the digital utility that connects 500 million Indians.
author: Diaspora Desk
